clue.text: Yes, back to the sunburn for Chabad philosophy

parts.note: a tan is the browning of skin by the sun

indicators.note: back tells us the word for yes is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: ay is an old and dialect word for yes

explanation.surface: Someone says yes and turns to a sunburnt listener during a talk on Hasidic thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the old word for yes; 'to the sunburn' attaches it after the word for a suntan. The Tanya is the core text of the Chabad Hasidic movement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tanya is the foundational book of Chabad Hasidic thought, written by Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.

clue.text: Scurrilous slave sits there, stirring it up

indicators.note: stirring things up mixes them, so the letters of the two words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A foul-mouthed servant lounges about, causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirring it up' looks like the slave's mischief but is the anagram signal. Thersites is the railing common soldier of the Iliad, 'a deformed and scurrilous Greek' in Troilus and Cressida, where Ajax calls him a slave.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer and Shakespeare both portray this low-born Greek as a foul-tongued railer whom his betters treat as a slave.

clue.text: "Very cautious in her replies to his inquiries after her" (Ann Radcliffe, The Italian)

definitions.text: "Very cautious in her replies to his inquiries after her" (Ann Radcliffe, The Italian)

parts.words: "Very cautious in her replies to his inquiries after her" (Ann Radcliffe, The Italian)
parts.note: the quotation from Radcliffe's Gothic novel breaks off before the relative being asked about; the solver supplies that missing word

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in quotation: in The Italian the person cautiously answering is asked about a young female relative, the heroine Ellena.
explanation.definitionFit: The word completing the sentence is a female relative, the daughter of one's brother or sister.

clue.text: Moore protagonist, badly atrophied

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of the following word are put together wrongly, in another order

explanation.surface: A character in a novel by Moore has wasted away terribly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges ATROPHIED. George Moore wrote the novel Aphrodite in Aulis (1930).
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of love gives her name to George Moore's late novel and is its central figure.

clue.text: Her casual letters could reveal a king of Macedon

indicators.note: the letters of the preceding words, rearranged, could show something else, so they are to be reordered

explanation.surface: A woman's offhand correspondence might expose a royal secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters could reveal' rearranges HER CASUAL. 'Letters' looks like correspondence but means the individual letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Archelaus I ruled ancient Macedon around 413 to 399 BC and was patron of Euripides.

clue.text: "Apart from my —, my memory's very good" (Jean Anouilh)

definitions.text: "Apart from my —, my memory's very good" (Jean Anouilh)

parts.words: "Apart from my —, my memory's very good" (Jean Anouilh)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation: the blank is a condition whose name makes the remark comically self-defeating

explanation.walkthrough: The line, from Anouilh, is a paradox: the gap names a loss of memory, so the speaker's boast undoes itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the medical term for loss of memory, which sits absurdly beside a claim of good recall.

clue.text: Possibly sues (sic) in the name of Hecuba's father

indicators.note: possibly means the letters might be arranged in some other way, so the fodder is rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone may be taking legal action, quoted exactly, on behalf of a Trojan queen's parent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges SUES SIC; the '(sic)' looks like an editor's mark but supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In Euripides and Virgil, Cisseus is the Thracian king named as the father of Hecuba, Priam's queen.

clue.text: Point level, wipe it out

parts.note: E, east, is one of the compass points
to rase (a variant of raze) is to level a building to the ground

explanation.surface: Flatten the point of the argument and rub it away.
explanation.walkthrough: RASE is the older spelling of raze, to knock flat.
explanation.definitionFit: To delete or rub something away is to obliterate it completely.

clue.text: Grand month in England for Algerian saint

parts.note: august means grand or majestic, and it is also the name of a summer month

explanation.surface: A North African holy man spends a splendid summer month in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand month' is one piece: the adjective august (grand) that is also a month.
explanation.definitionFit: St Augustine was bishop of Hippo Regius, the modern Annaba in Algeria.

clue.text: Sea nymph shows anger from pole to pole

indicators.note: anger reaching from one pole to the other spans the space between them, so it sits inside

parts.note: S, south, is one magnetic or geographic pole
N, north, is the other pole
ire is a literary word for anger

explanation.surface: A mermaid displays fury across the whole globe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from pole to pole' has IRE stretching between S and N, the two poles.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sirens of Greek myth were sea creatures who lured sailors to wreck with song.

clue.text: Agatha Christie's could remember

parts.note: reads as a remark about what Christie's characters recalled, but it is the title of her Poirot novel with its middle word changed

explanation.walkthrough: Christie's late Poirot novel is Elephants Can Remember (1972); the clue swaps 'can' for 'could'.
explanation.definitionFit: The animals proverbially said never to forget give the title of Christie's 1972 novel.

clue.text: American author appears in final geriatric offering ()

indicators.note: the answer appears inside the run of letters across the next two words

explanation.surface: A writer from the United States turns up in the last offering to the elderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears in' points to the letters spanning finAL GERiatric; 'offering' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio Alger was a nineteenth-century American writer of rags-to-riches novels for boys.

clue.text: First simple, very easy verse of Italian novelist ()

indicators.note: first tells us to take the opening letter of each of the following words in turn

explanation.surface: Opening lines of plain, easy verse by an Italian writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' takes the initials of simple, very, easy, verse, of.
explanation.definitionFit: Italo Svevo, of Trieste, wrote the novel Zeno's Conscience.

clue.text: His fellow traveller was an ass

definitions.text: His fellow traveller was an ass

parts.words: His fellow traveller was an ass
parts.note: sounds like an insult about a companion, but the companion was literally a donkey on a walking tour in France

explanation.surface: Someone's travelling companion was a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes (1879) records a walk with the donkey Modestine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish author of Treasure Island wrote of crossing the Cévennes with a donkey as companion.

clue.text: Catherine was such a big wheel

definitions.text: Catherine was such a big wheel

parts.words: Catherine was such a big wheel
parts.note: a big wheel is an important person; Catherine the Great of Russia held the highest rank of all

explanation.surface: Catherine was very important.
explanation.walkthrough: Catherine the Great was a Russian empress; 'big wheel' hints too at the Catherine wheel firework.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian empress, the title Catherine the Great held, ranked as the most powerful figure in the empire.

clue.text: A preposition bad to end a sentence with? — a rule up with which Churchill would not put, yet which some writers may

definitions.text: A preposition bad to end a sentence with? — a rule up with which Churchill would not put, yet which some writers may

parts.words: A preposition bad to end a sentence with? — a rule up with which Churchill would not put, yet which some writers may
parts.note: the clue debates the rule against ending a sentence with a preposition; some writers may consent to the rule, using a phrasal verb that itself ends in a preposition

explanation.surface: A grammar quarrel about the rule Churchill mocked with 'up with which I will not put'.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke attributed to Churchill mocks the rule; the answer is what some writers may do with it, a two-word verb that ends in a preposition itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept or settle on a rule jointly is to consent to it, which some writers do with this grammatical one.

clue.text: Sort of prose by which one may be swayed, we hear

definitions.text: Sort of prose by which one may be swayed, we hear

parts.words: Sort of prose by which one may be swayed, we hear
parts.note: describes writing that wins readers over, and the opening of the word sounds like sway

explanation.surface: A kind of writing that wins its readers over.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Latin suadere, to persuade; 'swayed, we hear' points at how its first syllable sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing that urges acceptance and wins people over is described with this formal adjective.

clue.text: Athenian spiritual brother of ID

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Athenian spiritual brother of ID': APEMANTUS is the Cynic of Timon of Athens, but 'ID' gives no sense or letters as held (likely an OCR garble of a name such as Diogenes); no scan to confirm.

clue.text: Devotees of the novel, visiting this play, may not see the Wood for the adapters' work

definitions.text: Devotees of the novel, visiting this play, may not see the Wood for the adapters' work

parts.words: Devotees of the novel, visiting this play, may not see the Wood for the adapters' work
parts.note: twists 'not see the wood for the trees': stage adaptations of a famous Victorian novel by Mrs Henry Wood buried her original

explanation.walkthrough: The novel was by Ellen Wood, published as Mrs Henry Wood (1861); its many melodrama versions gave the line 'Dead, and never called me mother!', not in the book.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen Wood's sensation novel became one of the most performed Victorian stage melodramas.

clue.text: Victorian novelist on French river

parts.note: sur is the French word for on
the Tees is a river in north-east England

explanation.surface: A nineteenth-century writer sits beside a river in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on French' means the French for 'on'; the Tees is a river in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Smith Surtees wrote the Jorrocks hunting novels in the 1830s to 1860s.

clue.text: French friends supporting girl in naval battle

indicators.note: in a down answer a supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes after the other

parts.note: Sal is a short form of the girl's name Sally
amis is French for friends

explanation.surface: Friends from France back a young woman in a battle at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supporting' puts AMIS below SAL in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: At Salamis in 480 BC the Greek fleet defeated the Persians in a famous sea fight.

clue.text: Invulnerable Thessalonian hero seen about east-north east to us

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about
ENE is the compass abbreviation for east-north-east

explanation.surface: A hero who cannot be wounded is spotted heading in a compass direction towards us.
explanation.walkthrough: CA (circa, about), ENE and US are joined in order; 'seen' and 'to' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Caeneus, a Lapith of Thessaly in Greek myth, was made invulnerable to weapons by Poseidon.

clue.text: Four-legged master of the healing arts with Precepts recorded by Hesiod

definitions.text: Four-legged master of the healing arts with Precepts recorded by Hesiod

parts.words: Four-legged master of the healing arts with Precepts recorded by Hesiod
parts.note: describes the wise centaur who taught medicine, whose Precepts were a lost didactic poem attributed to Hesiod

explanation.walkthrough: The centaur tutored Asclepius in medicine; the Precepts of Chiron, attributed to Hesiod, survive only in fragments.
explanation.definitionFit: This centaur of Greek myth, half horse, was teacher of heroes and of the healer Asclepius.

clue.text: Tennyson offered him revenge after defeat

definitions.text: Tennyson offered him revenge after defeat

parts.words: Tennyson offered him revenge after defeat
parts.note: reads as vengeance, but Revenge was the name of the ship in Tennyson's ballad, whose captain died after his famous last fight

explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's ballad The Revenge (1878) tells how Sir Richard Grenville's ship fought a Spanish fleet off the Azores in 1591.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Richard Grenville commanded the Revenge in the 1591 battle that Tennyson's ballad celebrates.

clue.text: Caesar's librarian, from Young Lochinvar (rough translation)

indicators.note: from tells us the answer is taken out of the letters of the next words

explanation.surface: Caesar's book-keeper turns up in a rough translation of Scott's ballad Young Lochinvar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points to the letters spanning LochinVAR (ROugh; 'Young' and 'translation' are surface dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Julius Caesar chose the scholar Marcus Terentius Varro to organise Rome's first public library.

clue.text: He suggested control at the middle, the biggest part, according to Huxley's savage

definitions.text: He suggested control at the middle, the biggest part, according to Huxley's savage

parts.words: He suggested control at the middle, the biggest part, according to Huxley's savage
parts.note: control at the middle is a girdle, and the biggest part is the earth's circumference; the Savage in Brave New World recalls Shakespeare's spirit promising to put a girdle round the earth

explanation.walkthrough: In Brave New World, John the Savage, steeped in Shakespeare, recalls the Tempest spirit's boast of putting a girdle round the earth in forty minutes (a line Puck also speaks).
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero's airy spirit in The Tempest is the figure the Savage associates with circling the globe.

clue.text: Nymph has concept about article

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for concept is placed around the article

parts.note: an idea is a concept
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A nymph has a notion about something written in the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts IDEA around A.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaea was a nymph of Mount Ida in Greek myth, mother of Teucer.

clue.text: Use caps in this case ()

parts.note: in typesetting, capitals are kept in one of the two cases of type, the higher one

explanation.surface: Wear hats on this occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: Compositors kept capitals in the top case of type, hence the term for capital letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital letters are called the top case, the higher of the compositor's two type trays.

clue.text: Observe the couple who wrote of innocents abroad

parts.note: to mark something is to notice or observe it
twain is an old word for two, a couple

explanation.surface: Watch the pair who wrote about naive tourists overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: Twain is archaic for two; The Innocents Abroad (1869) is his travel book.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Clemens, writing as this pen name, published The Innocents Abroad about Americans touring Europe.

clue.text: Rare poet, but identified with every man

definitions.text: Rare poet, but identified with every man

parts.words: Rare poet, but identified with every man
parts.note: 'O rare' is the epitaph on this poet's tomb, and Every Man in His Humour is his comedy

explanation.surface: An unusual poet who nevertheless represents everybody.
explanation.walkthrough: His Westminster Abbey gravestone reads 'O rare Ben Jonson'; his plays include Every Man in His Humour and Every Man out of His Humour.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jacobean playwright and poet is remembered by his famous epitaph and his Every Man comedies.

clue.text: Lawrence encountered one in his pyjamas by Tantalus

definitions.text: Lawrence encountered one in his pyjamas by Tantalus

parts.words: Lawrence encountered one in his pyjamas by Tantalus
parts.note: in his poem a creature came to D. H. Lawrence's water-trough in Sicily as he stood there in pyjamas in the heat; the creature drank, which water fled from Tantalus

explanation.walkthrough: D. H. Lawrence's poem tells of meeting a creature at his water-trough in Taormina 'in pyjamas for the heat'; Tantalus could never drink the water around him.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence's 1923 poem describes this reptile coming to drink, and his shame at throwing a log at it.
